In his third week at the Gurugram insurance office, Jeevan heard it again. At the coffee machine, a colleague put on a thick Kannada accent: "Yenri, sir, coffee strong-aa?" Two others laughed.

Jeevan laughed along, then went back to his desk and stared at the same spreadsheet for twenty minutes. He had topped his university. Here, he'd started talking less in meetings.

Mahima, from claims, pulled up a chair at lunch. "That coffee thing. It happens to you a lot, doesn't it?"

He nodded. Saying it out loud made his throat tight. "I thought maybe I was being too sensitive."

"You're not. It's mockery."

The next time it happened, Jeevan said evenly, "Please don't imitate my accent. It's not funny to me." The colleague rolled his eyes but stopped. When it started up again a week later, Jeevan and Mahima wrote it up for HR together.

That evening, on the phone to his mother, he spoke in Kannada for an hour, and didn't lower his voice.

qa.a: "Yenri, sir, coffee strong-aa?"

qa.a: He felt hurt and shaken, starting to doubt himself and speak less in meetings.

Dear Trisha,

You asked how Melbourne really is. Mostly good. But I want to tell you something I haven't told Amma.

In my share house, one of the flatmates keeps saying things like, "You people must love spicy food, right?" and "Your English is so good for an Indian." Last week they had a barbecue and didn't invite me. I heard it through my wall.

I cried, then felt stupid for crying. Then I started wondering if my English actually was bad.

It isn't. I know that now. My lab partner, who's from Chile, sat with me and said, "They've decided who you are before meeting you. That's their problem." I've started eating dinners with her and her friends.

I also told my flatmate, calmly, that the comments aren't compliments. The landlord knows about it too, in writing, in case it gets worse.

Write back soon. I miss your laugh.

Jaya

qa.a: "Your English is so good for an Indian."

Dear Parveen,

Four months in Osaka! I promised to tell you everything, so here goes.

Everyone takes off their shoes at the door, even at some offices. I love it now. Our flat will be a no-shoes flat when I'm back, warn Ammi. 😄

At work, meetings are so quiet. People don't interrupt. At first I thought nobody liked my ideas. Now I've learned to send my points in writing before the meeting, and they actually get discussed. I'm keeping that habit forever.

Food: I've eaten raw fish, fermented beans and something I still can't name. Some I loved. The beans, never again.

But I haven't changed everything. I still do my namaz in the small room at the station, and on Fridays I bring biryani for my team. Last week my manager asked for the recipe.

I'm learning a lot. I'm also still very much your cousin Leela.

Irawati's diary. Bengaluru. Late.

Papa fell in the bathroom in Indore this morning. He's fine, only a bruise, but I heard it from Kamal-uncle next door, not from Papa. Papa said on the phone, "Why worry you for nothing?"

I sat at my desk after the call and cried. I'm six hundred kilometres away building a career while my parents get older without me. Should I quit and go home? I love this job. I love them more. It feels like choosing.

But crying at my desk isn't helping them.

So tonight I made a list. Video call every evening at eight, not just Sundays. Book a trip home for Diwali now, not "sometime." Ask Kamal-uncle if he'd check on them each morning, and pay a local helper to come in daily. Tell Papa honestly that I'd rather know about small falls than find out later.

Love can travel, I think. It just needs a timetable.

qa.a: Kamal-uncle next door.

qa.a: Irawati felt guilty and torn between loving the job and loving the parents more, crying at the desk.

qa.a: Irawati planned daily calls, booked a Diwali trip, arranged a morning check and a helper, and asked Papa for honesty, turning guilt into action.

"Fine, Papa. How are you?"

"All good, all good. Your mother made kadhi. Very tasty."

Ganga paused. Papa never talked about kadhi. "Papa, are you actually okay? Honestly."

A silence. "The house is quiet, beti. That's all. We keep setting three plates."

Ganga's eyes filled. "I miss you both too. Listen. Can I video call during your evening walk tomorrow? I'll show you my office canteen. It's terrible."

"And Papa, I'm deciding whether to take the Pune posting next year. I want your opinion."

"Mine?" He sounded surprised, and pleased. "Let me think. I'll tell you Sunday."

"And if Mummy's knee gets worse, you tell me. I'll come."

"I'll tell you," he said, and his voice sounded real now.

I'm Pallavi, and I almost missed it.

When I moved to Delhi, Amma called every Sunday sounding perfectly happy. "Everything is fine, kanna. Don't worry about us." I believed her, because it was easy to.

Then my neighbour back home, Yamini-aunty, messaged me: "Your mother has stopped coming to the temple group. She says she's tired."

Amma loved that group.

On Sunday I didn't let her say "fine." I asked, "Amma, what did you do on Tuesday? Who did you talk to?" It came out slowly. Since I'd left, she didn't see the point of cooking properly, or going out.

I started sending her small things: photos of my lunch, voice notes from the bus. I asked her advice about my flat curtains. And for Pongal I went home, not for two days but a full week.

She still says she's fine. Now I know how to ask.

qa.a: Yamini-aunty, a neighbour back home.

qa.a: Amma was likely lonely and sad, missing Pallavi and losing interest in cooking and going out.

Welcome to Dubai! Your uncle told me you landed last week and are staying in Karama. When I arrived three years ago, the Telugu association found me a room, lent me a winter jacket for the office AC, and fed me pulihora at every festival. I owe them a lot, so here is my turn.

But I'll also say what someone should have told me. For my first year, all my friends were Telugu. It was comfortable, and it kept me small. Now I play football with a Filipino and Egyptian team on Tuesdays, and I've learnt more from them than from any year before.

So come for pulihora. Then go find people who've never tasted it.

Call me anytime.
Deepak

The Tamil group saved me. Seriously. Someone met me at the station. Someone else found my first flat. At Pongal, forty of us crammed into a church hall and I cried into my sakkarai pongal.

So I joined a hiking club. Terrible German at first. They laughed at my accent and then taught me the right words. Now I have friends from four countries.

And last month a new student from Madurai messaged the group, lost and scared. I picked her up from the airport. That felt like closing a circle.

Stay close to our people. Just don't stop there."

Harish had come from Guwahati to work at a garment unit in Bengaluru. On day one, the supervisor took his original ID documents "for safekeeping." By month two, twelve-hour days were normal, and overtime never showed up on his payslip.

When he asked for his documents to open a bank account, the supervisor said, "Later. You'll run away otherwise."

Harish's hands went cold. He called Pallavi, a volunteer at a workers' helpline whose number was on a poster at the bus stop.

"First, do you have copies of anything?" she asked.

"Photos on my phone."

"Good. Keep them safe, and email them to yourself. Write down your hours every day. Tomorrow, come to our legal aid clinic. Holding your documents isn't allowed. We'll help you ask for them back properly."

That night Harish emailed the photos, wrote a list of every shift he could remember, and slept a little.

Sabina had grown up in London and came back to her grandmother's village near Malappuram for the first time in ten years. The cousins called her "the English one." In London, people had asked where she was really from.

At the well, the older women spoke too fast for her rusty Malayalam. She smiled, understood half, and felt like a visitor in her own family.

Her cousin Varun found her sitting alone on the veranda. "You're sad."

"I'm not from here and I'm not from there. I don't know what I am."

Varun shrugged. "The kids at the tuition centre want to practise English for their exams. You're the only one who can help them and still understand their Malayalam jokes."

The next afternoon she taught twelve children. When she got a word wrong in Malayalam, they corrected her, laughing. She kept a notebook of new words.

That evening she felt, for once, useful to both halves of herself.

Sami left the clinic in Helsinki holding a folder he couldn't read through the blur in his eyes. The doctor had said "tumour," then a lot of other words he had lost.

At home, Sami did what he'd promised himself not to: he searched. At 2 a.m. he was reading forums with the worst stories on the internet, his heart pounding.

Mateo, his partner, found him on the kitchen floor. He closed the laptop gently. "Not tonight. Come to bed."

In the morning they sat together and wrote a list of questions. What stage is it? What are the options? What happens first? Mateo asked for the next appointment so he could come too.

At the clinic Mateo took notes while Sami asked. The doctor answered each one and offered to arrange a second opinion. One step at a time, she said.

On the tram home Sami read the notes. Still frightening. But now it had edges.

The waiting area of the oncology ward in Kochi smelled of antiseptic and jasmine from someone's hair. Vidya sat with her brother Hrithik, the new report folded in her lap.

Last week the first doctor had said "surgery soon" in a rush, and she had nodded because she was too scared to ask anything. That night she'd barely slept.

This time Hrithik had made her write questions in a small notebook. "You ask. I'll write the answers," he said.

The second doctor was slower. Vidya read from her notebook, voice shaking. What exactly is the diagnosis? What are the choices? What happens if we wait a little? The doctor answered each one and said a second opinion was wise.

Walking out, Vidya's hands were still cold. But she had the answers in Hrithik's handwriting and a plan for the next step.

"One thing at a time," Hrithik said, holding the door.

Dear Dr. Kiran,

I'm writing to say thank you, because I never managed it in the clinic.

When you first told me about the kidney disease, you drew the kidneys on the back of a form and explained everything. The choices, the risks, what we didn't know yet. You didn't make it sound easy. That was why I believed you.

I'll admit I didn't tell you everything at first. I hadn't mentioned the painkillers I'd been taking from the chemist. You asked again, kindly, and when I told you, you changed the plan.

I've kept every appointment since. I write my questions in a notebook, and when I didn't understand the diet chart, I asked twice, and you explained twice.

I don't just follow the plan. I feel like part of it.

With gratitude,
Darshan

"You asked how I stayed sane during treatment. I'm Wasim, and a lot of it was Dr. Gopika.

When I was diagnosed, I was twenty-five and angry and I didn't trust any doctor. The first one I saw talked over my head to my father.

Dr. Gopika spoke to me. She put the scan on the screen and said, 'Here's what we know, here's what we don't, and here are three choices.' She even told me which one she'd pick and why, and said I could get another opinion.

But I also learned to ask. When a word confused me, I said, 'Explain that again.' When I didn't agree, I said so.

Trust isn't just saying yes. It's showing up as a partner."

Payal, twenty-four, finished her third cycle today. During the drip she threw the water jug against the wall and shouted at her mother, "Stop hovering! Just go home!" Her mother left the room in tears.

Afterwards Payal cried. "Why me? I run marathons. I never even smoke. It's not fair."

I sat with her. I said her anger made complete sense: this illness had taken control of her body, her plans, her year. I also said the jug and the shouting had landed on the person who sleeps on a chair by her bed every night.

She asked what she could do with the anger instead. We talked about the art room on Thursdays, and writing letters she never sends. She said she might try walking the corridor when it rises.

Before leaving, she asked me to bring her mother back in. They held each other for a long time.

Karthik, staff nurse

qa.a: The water jug.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she cried afterwards?
qa.a: She felt bitter and angry at the unfairness of her illness, asking "Why me?" and feeling it was not fair.

qa.q: What did Karthik suggest, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: Karthik accepted the anger as natural, pointed out it was landing on her mother, and suggested the art room, unsent letters or walking, which gave the anger safer outlets.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother see the outburst?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt hurt and pushed away, leaving in tears, but relieved when Payal asked for her back.

Ojas. Diary. Friday night.

Swati drove me to the hospital again today and I was awful to her. She asked if I'd eaten and I snapped, "Stop treating me like a child." She went quiet the whole drive back.

I'm twenty-six. Everyone my age is getting promotions and going on trips. I'm counting tablets and losing hair. Why me? It's so unfair I want to scream.

The counsellor at the clinic said anger makes sense when you lose control of your life. She said to put it somewhere safe. So here it is, diary. I'm furious. I hate this illness. I hate that I can't plan next month.

I also went for a slow walk round the block after dinner, and punched my pillow twice. It helped a bit.

Then I texted Swati: "I'm sorry about the car. I'm angry at being sick, not at you. Thank you for driving me."

She replied with a heart.

qa.a: "Stop treating me like a child."

qa.a: Ojas felt furious and bitter, finding it unfair that others were getting promotions while Ojas was counting tablets.

qa.a: Writing in the diary, a slow walk round the block and punching a pillow, then apologising to Swati.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt after Ojas snapped at her?
qa.a: Swati probably felt hurt and quiet on the drive, and then relieved and touched by the apology, replying with a heart.
